This means three separate, real documented threads (Clinton-Summers-Epstein; Barak-Epstein directly; Barak referencing Summers to Epstein) all touch Summers' name — a genuine convergence of a small, real social world, not a document showing all three men interacting as a group or coordinating anything.
- **billclinton**: Discipline — What the Record Shows and Does Not Shows: a real, mappable 2° network path from Clinton to Epstein via Barak, and a documented convergence around Larry Summers' name specifically. Does not show: that Clinton had any awareness of, or connection to, Barak's own extensive and separately-documented Epstein relationship — the timelines barely overlap, and no document connects the two men's separate contacts with Epstein to each other. Per this project's standing rule, adjacency through a shared acquaintance is not evidence of awareness, coordination, or shared conduct.
- **billclinton**: Britannica's own summary states Clinton knew Epstein 'at least as early as 1993,' when Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell were photographed with Clinton at a White House Historical Association event — corroborated by the Clinton Presidential Library's own archived photo, not a single contested source. In his 2026 sworn testimony, Clinton told the committee he first recalls meeting Epstein in 2002, aboard his plane — a more specific claim than his earlier, more careful public framing ('not a specific interaction' during 1993–2001). This module notes rather than resolves the tension: a brief 1993 photo-op at a large donor event and a substantive relationship beginning in 2001–02 (per Larry Summers' introduction, by Clinton's own account) aren't strictly contradictory, but the 2026 testimony's specificity about 2002 sits awkwardly next to the corroborated 1993 photo.
- **bank**: Sponsored by Sen. Phil Gramm (R-TX), Rep. Jim Leach (R-IA), and Rep. Thomas Bliley (R-VA) — a Republican-led Congress — signed by President Bill Clinton (D), with documented support from Greenspan, Rubin, and Rubin's successor Lawrence Summers. Repealed the remaining Glass-Steagall restrictions entirely, legally validating the Citigroup merger after the fact and opening the mega-bank era.
- **bank**: CFTC Chair Brooksley Born raised early public warnings about unregulated derivatives markets, particularly credit default swaps. She was directly opposed by Greenspan, Rubin, and Summers — one meeting reportedly ended with Rubin asking, 'You're not going to do anything, right?' Born left the CFTC in 1999. The following year, Sen. Gramm pushed the Commodity Futures Modernization Act, exempting derivatives from CFTC/SEC oversight — passed with no floor debate, attached as a rider to an 11,000-page spending bill, the day after the Supreme Court effectively decided the 2000 election. Outstanding derivatives grew from $106 trillion (2001) to $531 trillion (2008).
- **bank**: It did. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act passed a Republican-led Congress in 1999 and was signed by President Clinton — with documented support from Greenspan, Rubin, and Rubin's successor Lawrence Summers — legally validating the merger after the fact. Citigroup, the result, was at the time the largest corporate merger in history. The bank remains, today, one of the largest issuing banks referenced throughout this simulation's overdraft and interchange revenue data (Scene 14, 21).
